partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a ground-floor flat. In August 2023, they contacted the landlord to ask when it would complete repairs to the render at the rear of the property and to a brick pillar in the front garden. The resident complained about delays in repairs to the external render and a brick pillar on 31 July 2024. They said the issues had been ongoing since January 2020 and expressed frustration with the delays and the landlord's poor communication. The landlord upheld the complaint on 3 September 2024, explaining that render repairs were identified in August 2023, but a recent inspection found the render did not require replacement. However, due to flaking paint, redecoration works would be raised for consideration under its planned investment programme. The brick pillar was removed for safety reasons and the rebuild was scheduled for September 2024. The landlord offered £50 for complaint handling failures, £50 under the right-to-repair scheme relating to the brick pillar delays, and £300 for delays and inconvenience caused by the repair delays. The resident escalated their complaint the same day as they were dissatisfied with the compensation offered and the repair delays. The landlord issued its stage 2 response on 11 October 2024, confirming that the brick pillar was repaired on 17 September 2024, and awarded an additional £250 for its failures, increasing the total compensation offer to £650.
partial_case.ground_truth_outcome: Service failure in handling of external repairs; Reasonable redress in complaint handling

key_reasoning_quotes.text: By the time it issued its final complaint response, the landlord had rebuilt the brick pillar and assessed that the render did not require replacement. It acknowledged failures in its handling of the repairs and offered appropriate compensation for the delays and failures leading to completion. However, it has not provided an appropriate remedy for failing to complete the actions it had committed to in its complaint responses.

While the landlord sought to put things right during its complaints procedure, it did not fulfil all the commitments made in its complaint responses (as identified above). Its total compensation offer of £550 did not account for this. On this basis, there was service failure in its handling of the external repairs.

partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a ground-floor flat and contacted the landlord in August 2023 about repairs to rear render and a front-garden brick pillar. The complaint concerned external repairs to the property render and a garden brick pillar, and the associated complaint. On 31 July 2024, the resident complained about delays in repairs to the external render and brick pillar, saying the issues had been ongoing since January 2020 and expressing frustration with delays and poor communication. On 3 September 2024, the landlord issued a complaint response addressing render repairs, the brick pillar, planned investment consideration, delay, poor communication and compensation offers. The resident escalated the complaint on 3 September 2024 because they were dissatisfied with the compensation offered and the repair delays. On 11 October 2024, the landlord issued its stage 2 response, confirmed the brick pillar was repaired on 17 September 2024, arranged a post-inspection for 30 October 2024, and increased the total compensation offer to £650. The resident referred the complaint to the Ombudsman because they felt the compensation offered did not reflect the extent of the delays and failures experienced.

orders: The landlord must pay the resident £650 for distress and inconvenience caused by its handling of the external repairs, including the £550 previously offered and an additional £100.
The landlord must refer the render decoration works for consideration under its planned investment programme and provide evidence of the referral.
ground_truth_outcome.recommendation: The landlord should pay the resident £100 as offered for its complaint handling failures if not already paid.

It acknowledged failures in its handling of the repairs and offered appropriate compensation for the delays and failures leading to completion. However, it has not provided an appropriate remedy for failing to complete the actions it had committed to in its complaint responses.
The landlord accepted failings in its handling of the resident’s complaints. It apologised and offered compensation, which was sufficient to put things right during the complaints procedure.

In this case, the landlord’s records do not explain the reasons for the delays or show what steps were taken to progress the works during these periods. It also failed to update the resident during these periods.
However, when we asked it to provide evidence of this referral, the landlord was unable to confirm whether it had been made.
Therefore, the landlord offered reasonable redress for its complaint handling failures.
